summary: Remote triggered black hole filtering discards attack traffic based on addresses. This informational RFC reserves a prefix, 100::/64, for IPv6 discard use and updates the IPv6 Special Purpose Address Registry.

plainLanguage.summary: One dead-end street is set aside where bad traffic is sent and thrown away.

questions: what is the ipv6 discard prefix
why not use documentation prefixes for discard filtering
subtitle: A reserved IPv6 prefix for filtering and discarding unwanted traffic.

tldr.problem: Networks use black hole filtering to drop attack traffic based on destination address, but were using unassigned or documentation address space for this, creating ambiguity about what prefixes should be reserved.
tldr.mechanism: IANA assigns a dedicated IPv6 prefix, 100::/64, as a Discard-Only Prefix specifically for remote triggered black hole filtering and routing.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use a globally consistent prefix for discard filtering, avoiding conflicts with documentation or private address ranges.

facts.label: Allocation
facts.value: IANA IPv6 Special Purpose Address Registry

today: RFC 6666 is an Internet Standard-track Informational RFC that formally reserves the IPv6 discard prefix. It is not superseded.

sections.title: Remote Triggered Black Hole Filtering
sections.content:
Remote triggered black hole (RTBH) filtering is a method of defending against denial-of-service attacks by selectively discarding traffic destined to a target address. When an attack is detected, routers are configured to direct traffic to that address into a discard interface or tunnel, preventing it from reaching the target.

Earlier, networks implemented RTBH systems by routing attack traffic to private address space (RFC 1918) or to documentation prefixes (RFC 5737). However, these approaches create operational confusion: documentation prefixes should be filtered in both local and public contexts, and private space is meant for private networks, not production defense infrastructure. There was no globally recognized standard prefix for this critical operational task.
sections.plainLanguage: When the internet is under attack, routers can automatically send the bad traffic down a special dead-end address so it does not hurt the real servers. This RFC gives everyone an official dead-end address.

sections.title: The Discard Prefix
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that IANA assign the IPv6 prefix 100::/64 (written as 0100::/64 in full IPv6 notation) as a dedicated Discard-Only Prefix. The /64 means the prefix covers a block of addresses from 100::0 to 100::ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff.

This size was chosen to allow multiple RTBH scenarios: as noted in earlier RFCs on RTBH, operators may need more than one discard address to implement different filtering policies or to separate different types of attacks. A full /64 block provides this flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The official dead-end address range is 100::/64, which is like a whole neighborhood of wrong addresses. It has enough room for many different discard scenarios.

sections.title: Deployment and Filtering
sections.content:
Operators may announce this prefix within their autonomous system using dynamic routing protocols like BGP. However, the prefix should not be announced to or accepted from third-party autonomous systems. If the prefix leaks into inter-domain BGP, traffic intended for discard might reach another network unintentionally, potentially amplifying a denial-of-service attack.

Within a network implementing IPv6 RTBH, routers can be configured with this prefix pointing to a discard or null interface, meaning packets destined to any address in 100::/64 are dropped immediately. BGP prefix filters should be configured to ensure this prefix does not escape the network boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network uses the discard prefix only on the inside, like a real dead-end street in your own town. You do not advertise it to other networks, so traffic never escapes.

sections.title: Standards Adoption and Impact
sections.content:
This RFC formalizes the allocation of a globally recognized discard prefix, ending the era of operators improvising with documentation or private address space. The specification resolves ambiguity about what prefix to use for RTBH implementations, making it possible for operators to deploy consistent defense mechanisms across their networks and coordinate with peers.

The discard prefix has been recorded in the IANA IPv6 Special Purpose Address Registry, making it an official part of the IPv6 address architecture. The key operational requirement is that this prefix be isolated within networks where RTBH is deployed: it must not leak into the global routing system, or inter-domain traffic to the discard prefix could cause unintended consequences. Proper BGP filtering and internal routing configuration are essential for safe deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: By creating an official dead-end address, the RFC lets everyone use the same one, and networks can coordinate to keep it from escaping to the internet.
